passages.t: Do not judge: the speck and the beam
passages.happening:
“Do not judge, or you will be judged” (verse 1). The measure you use for others will be used for you.

Then Jesus paints a funny and painful picture. Why look at the speck of sawdust in your brother's eye and not notice the beam in your own? How can you offer to take out his speck with a beam in your eye? “You hypocrite! First take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother's eye” (verse 5).

Then a short, strange saying: do not give what is holy to dogs, or throw your pearls before pigs, or they may trample them and turn on you (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
The ‘speck’ is a chip of straw or wood. The ‘beam’ is a roof timber. A carpenter's son would know both. The picture is meant to make people laugh: a man with a plank sticking out of his eye, offering to do delicate work on someone else's.

Jewish teachers knew a similar saying. The Babylonian Talmud, written down centuries later, tells of Rabbi Tarfon wondering whether anyone in his generation could accept a rebuke. If you tell someone to take the splinter from between his eyes, he answers, ‘Take the beam from between yours’ (Arakhin 16b).

In the Bible, dogs are mostly street scavengers, not pets (1 Kings 14:11), and the Law called pigs unclean (Leviticus 11:7). Pearls were costly; in a later parable a merchant sells everything he has for one (13:45-46). ‘What is holy’ may mean food set apart for God, which the Law said outsiders must not eat (Exodus 29:33). Feeding it to dogs, or pearls to pigs, would be waste and worse.
passages.ot: Think of someone whose faults you notice easily. Before you say anything, ask what might be stuck in your own eye. Then, if you still need to speak, go gently, as someone who has had a beam removed too.
passages.asks:
Do not judge? Does Jesus mean Christians may never say that anything is wrong? Most readers say no, and the passage itself shows why. In verse 5 Jesus expects the brother's speck to be removed, once your own eye is clear. In verse 6 he expects his followers to tell the difference between those who will receive something holy and those who will trample it. Elsewhere Jesus says, “If your brother sins against you, go and confront him privately” (18:15), and, “Stop judging by outward appearances, and start judging justly” (John 7:24).

What Jesus forbids is the judging that condemns, that looks down, that sees others' faults and never one's own. Paul says to restore someone who has fallen “with a spirit of gentleness” and to watch yourself (Galatians 6:1).

Who are the ‘dogs’ and ‘pigs’? ‘Dog’ could be a hard word for outsiders (see 15:26), but Matthew's Gospel ends with Jesus sending his followers to “all nations” (28:19), so most readers take the saying to be about people who mock what is holy, not about any people group. It is a word of wisdom about when to speak, not a license to look down on anyone.

passages.t: Ask, seek, knock; and the golden rule
passages.happening:
“Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened to you” (verse 7). Everyone who asks receives.

Which of you, if your son asks for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a snake? If you, though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father in heaven give good things to those who ask him?

Then comes the most famous rule of all: “In everything, then, do to others as you would have them do to you. For this is the essence of the Law and the Prophets” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Bread and fish were the everyday food of Galilee, around a lake full of fish. A round flat loaf might even look like a stone. Readers of Matthew may remember the devil asking Jesus to turn stones into bread (4:3). No father would trick his hungry child that way.

Jesus calls his hearers ‘evil’ in passing, as if it were obvious. Even flawed parents give good things. How much more the Father.

The ‘golden rule’ had cousins in Jewish teaching. The book of Tobit, written two or three centuries before Jesus, says, in effect, do not do to anyone what you hate. The Babylonian Talmud, written down much later, remembers the great teacher Hillel summing up the Law for a Gentile: what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor; that is the whole Law, and the rest is commentary (Shabbat 31a). Jesus states the rule in its positive form, and like Hillel he says it sums up the Law and the Prophets. Here Jesus and the best Jewish teachers of his day meet.
passages.ot:
Does Jesus promise that we will get whatever we ask for? A skeptic can fairly point to prayers that were not answered: the sick child who died, the marriage that ended. Some teachers have claimed that faith always brings health and money, and have blamed people when it did not. That is not what this passage teaches.

Read it in the sermon where Jesus put it. The prayer he gave in chapter 6 says, ‘Your will be done’, and asks only for daily bread. The Father ‘knows what you need before you ask Him’ (6:8). Here the promise is ‘good things’, and in Luke's version the gift is “the Holy Spirit” (Luke 11:13). A good father does not give a child everything the child asks for. In the garden Jesus himself prayed for the cup to pass, and then said, “Yet not as I will, but as You will” (26:39). Paul asked three times for his ‘thorn’ to be taken away and was told no (2 Corinthians 12:8-9). So most Christians read these words as a call to keep praying, to a Father who listens and gives what is good, not as a key to make God do what we want. The question of unanswered prayer is real, and this passage answers it with trust in a Father, not with a formula.
passages.hard: Is there something you stopped asking God for because the answer did not come? Jesus says keep knocking. And try the golden rule on one relationship this week. Before you speak or act, ask: how would I want to be treated here?
passages.asks: The rule grows out of “love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18). ‘The Law and the Prophets’ ties verse 12 back to 5:17, where Jesus said he came to fulfill them. The whole teaching in between is meant to be read as one piece, and this rule is its summary.

passages.happening: “Enter through the narrow gate. For wide is the gate and broad is the way that leads to destruction, and many enter through it” (verse 13). But small is the gate and narrow the way that leads to life, and only a few find it.
passages.hearers:
Two ways, one to life and one to death, was a familiar picture in Jewish teaching. Moses set before Israel “life and death, blessing and cursing” and told them, “Therefore choose life” (Deuteronomy 30:19). Psalm 1 ends with the two paths of the righteous and the wicked. Early Christians kept the picture. The Didache, a church handbook from around AD 100, opens by saying there are two ways, one of life and one of death, and a great difference between them.

A town gate was a real bottleneck. The broad road carries the crowd. The narrow way is the road Jesus has been describing in the whole sermon: humble, honest, merciful, loving even enemies. It is narrow not because God is stingy, but because few want to walk it.
passages.ot:
Does this mean most people will be lost? When someone asked Jesus, “will only a few people be saved?” he did not give a number. He said, “Make every effort to enter through the narrow door” (Luke 13:23-24). Some Christians read ‘many’ and ‘few’ as a warning not to follow the crowd, not a count of who will be saved. Others take the words as a sober statement that the saved will be fewer than the lost. Christians also differ on what final judgment is like, and these notes do not settle that here.

Skeptics raise a moral objection. The philosopher Bertrand Russell, in his 1927 lecture Why I Am Not a Christian, called Jesus' belief in hell a serious flaw in his moral character. Christians answer that Jesus warns because he loves, the way a guide warns of a cliff, and that the gate is open to anyone. The objection deserves an honest answer, not a quick one.

This verse is not meant to scare anyone into sleepless fear. It is an invitation: the gate is there, and it is open.
passages.hard: Where are you following the crowd simply because it is easier? The narrow way is not a test of how hard you can try. It is the road Jesus walks, and he walks it first. What would one step onto it look like for you this week?
passages.asks: Jeremiah brought God's word to Jerusalem: “I set before you the way of life and the way of death” (Jeremiah 21:8).

passages.happening: “Beware of false prophets. They come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves” (verse 15). You will know them by their fruit. People do not pick grapes from thornbushes or figs from thistles. A good tree bears good fruit and a bad tree bad fruit. Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.
passages.hearers:
False prophets were a real danger in Jesus' world. The Jewish historian Josephus tells of a man named Theudas who, in the AD 40s, called himself a prophet and led a crowd to the Jordan, promising that the river would part at his command. Roman cavalry killed many of them, and Theudas was beheaded (Antiquities 20.97-98). Acts also mentions a Theudas who ‘came to nothing’ (Acts 5:36).

The early church had to learn to tell true from false. The Didache gives practical tests for traveling prophets: one who stays three days, or who asks for money, is a false prophet.

Sheep and wolves came from everyday herding life. A wolf dressed as a sheep is the danger nobody sees coming. Thorns and thistles are the pair named in the curse on the ground after Adam's sin (Genesis 3:18).
passages.ot:
What counts as ‘fruit’? Readers have pointed to a teacher's life and character, what Paul calls “the fruit of the Spirit” (Galatians 5:22), and also to what the teaching produces in others over time. Gifts, crowds and success are not the test. In the next verses Jesus says some who do miracles are false.

This is not a call to suspect everyone, or to judge a person by one bad day. Fruit takes time to grow and to show. But it does mean a leader who uses people, demands money, or lives a hidden double life should not be trusted just because he speaks well or draws a crowd. Testing teachers is not disloyalty. Jesus commands it.
passages.hard: Whose voice shapes your faith most: a preacher, a writer, a channel, a friend? Look at the fruit. Does the teaching make people more humble, more honest, more loving? And look at your own life too. What fruit is it bearing?
passages.asks: The Law gave tests for prophets. A prophet who works a sign but leads people after other gods is false (Deuteronomy 13:1-3). A prophet whose word does not come true has not spoken from the LORD (Deuteronomy 18:22). Ezekiel called Jerusalem's corrupt officials wolves (Ezekiel 22:27). John the Baptist used the same tree picture: “every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (3:10).

passages.happening:
Not everyone who says to Jesus, ‘Lord, Lord’, will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only those who do the will of his Father.

On that day many will say, “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in Your name, and in Your name drive out demons and perform many miracles?” (verse 22). And Jesus will tell them plainly, ‘I never knew you; depart from Me, you workers of lawlessness’ (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
‘That day’ is the day of judgment, which the prophets called the day of the LORD. Here Jesus says he himself will be the one who speaks on that day. For a Jewish hearer that was a breathtaking claim: the judge at the end of history is the teacher on the hill.

The people in this scene are not outsiders. They call him ‘Lord’. They did remarkable things in his name. What is missing is not activity, but relationship and obedience. ‘Knew’ in the Bible often means more than knowing about someone. It means a close, personal bond. Jesus says, “I know My sheep and My sheep know Me” (John 10:14).

‘Lawlessness’ is a word Matthew uses for living as if God's commands do not matter. After a sermon about the Law fulfilled, it lands hard.
passages.ot:
This passage has frightened many sincere people. If people who did miracles are turned away, how can anyone be sure? Christian traditions answer in different ways. Many in the Reformed tradition stress that Jesus says he ‘never’ knew them, not that he once knew them and stopped, and that God's promises give real assurance to those who trust Christ. The Wesleyan tradition speaks of the Spirit's witness with our spirit, while warning that faith can be abandoned. Catholic teaching warns against presumption while commending firm hope in God's mercy. Across these views two things are shared.

First, the people in verse 22 rest their whole case on their own works: ‘did we not’. They never mention mercy. Second, Jesus' answer is not anxious self-examination. It is to hear his words and do them, and his words began with mercy for the poor in spirit (5:3). If you are afraid that you are one of the people in this verse, that fear is itself a sign that you care what Jesus thinks. Bring the fear to him. He also said, “Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest” (11:28).
passages.hard: Jesus is not asking how busy you are for him. He is asking whether you know him and do what he says. If you are tired from trying to earn his welcome, stop and rest in it. If you have been calling him ‘Lord’ without listening, start with one thing he said in these chapters and do it.
passages.asks: Luke gives a shorter form: “Why do you call Me ‘Lord, Lord,’ but not do what I say?” (Luke 6:46).

passages.t: Two builders, and a teacher with authority
passages.happening:
Jesus ends the sermon with a story. Everyone who hears these words of his and acts on them is like a wise man who built his house on the rock. The rain fell, the rivers rose, the winds beat against the house, and it did not fall. Everyone who hears and does not act is like a foolish man who built on sand. The same storm came, and the house fell, and great was its fall.

When Jesus finished, the crowds were astonished, “because He taught as one who had authority, and not as their scribes” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
Israel's rains came in their seasons (Deuteronomy 11:14), and a heavy storm could send torrents through low ground. A house on loose sand would be undercut. Luke says the wise builder “dug down deep and laid his foundation on the rock” (Luke 6:48). From the outside, both houses may have looked the same. Only the storm showed the difference.

Jewish teachers told similar stories. A later collection, Avot de-Rabbi Natan, has a parable about a man with good deeds and much study of the Law, who is like a builder who lays stones first and bricks on top, so that floods cannot move the house. Who first said it is uncertain, and the collection was written down long after the Gospels. Jesus' story belongs to that world of Jewish wisdom, with one difference: the rock is ‘these words of Mine’.

Why were the crowds amazed? Later Jewish teaching valued handing on what earlier teachers had received. The Mishnah, written down around AD 200, begins its sayings of the fathers with a chain: Moses received the Law at Sinai and passed it to Joshua, Joshua to the elders, and so on (Avot 1:1). Jesus quotes no teacher in this whole sermon. He says, ‘But I tell you.’
passages.ot:
Is Jesus teaching that we are saved by our good deeds? Christians have answered carefully. The sermon began with God's gift to the poor in spirit, and the Lord's Prayer asks for forgiveness. Most traditions say that God's grace comes first and that real faith shows itself in doing what Jesus says. Hearing alone, without doing, is the house on sand. Christians differ on how to describe the link between faith and works, but none of them treats Jesus' words as optional.

The ways Christians have read the whole Sermon on the Mount, as a pattern for every believer, as a higher calling, as two kinds of duty, as words to be taken literally, as a mirror that shows our need, or as a picture of the age to come, are set out on Matthew's book page, in the part called ‘The Sermon on the Mount, and how Christians have read it’.
passages.hard: Which words from these three chapters have you heard many times but never really acted on? Pick one. Storms come to every house, whether built on rock or on sand. The question Jesus leaves is not whether you have heard him, but what you are building on.
passages.asks: Ezekiel warned false prophets that a flimsy wall, whitewashed to look strong, would fall when the “Rain will come in torrents” (Ezekiel 13:11). Jesus' story uses the same pictures of rain, flood and wind.
